content:
Two new features of the Apple Watch may violate privacy laws in multiple US states, as the new Live Rewind and Siri Recap features will record conversations.

The devil is in the details—both features do not allow anyone to access the recordings, and it appears that court tests will be needed to establish new legal precedents......

Live Rewind and Siri Recap

Apple announced that its latest Apple Watch model supports four audio smart features using a built-in microphone:

  • Sound recognition, which can identify sounds such as doorbells and smoke alarms
  • Music recognition, powered by Shazam technology
  • Live Rewind, which converts conversations you just missed into text
  • Siri Recap, which provides high-level summaries of conversations

It is precisely the latter two features that have sparked privacy controversy, because they record what you and everyone around you say.

Recording-related laws

The legality and applicable timing of recording depends on the state or country you are in.

Many US states adopt so-called "two-party consent" rules, meaning that everyone in the conversation must know that the conversation is being recorded and give their consent. In these states, if you use any device to record a conversation without the other party's knowledge or consent, it is illegal. (Law enforcement agencies have some exceptions, but these are not relevant to this discussion.)

If the Apple Watch truly stores recordings and they can be played back, the laws in these states are clear: consent must be obtained first. The complexity lies in the fact that Apple has explicitly stated that this is not the case.

Apple's privacy measures

Apple has clearly put a lot of thought into privacy, and we previously discussed how they introduced each feature.

Neither feature runs in the background by default and must be manually activated each time. Live Rewind must be restarted each time it is used, and it only runs for 15 seconds. The recordings cannot be accessed by anyone and are only stored on a separate secure chip.

Recordings are only stored briefly and are deleted immediately after being used to generate a text transcript or summary.

Legal uncertainty

Despite the above measures, Bloomberg cited legal experts pointing out that these new features have introduced legal uncertainty.

Bloomberg reporter Natalie Lung consulted lawyers in California, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Washington state on September 11. These states generally prohibit the wiretapping of private or confidential conversations without the consent of all participants... Without exception, none of the lawyers she interviewed believed that Apple's safeguards could provide wearers with sufficient liability protection... Even if conversations are only continuously processed and ultimately produce no traditional recording, they may still be considered wiretapping under state law. Phil Lauer, a defense attorney in Pennsylvania, said the technology is "close to legal because in reality no individual is receiving and using this data." But he added that "it could still be deemed illegal" because the device is collecting and interpreting audio. Lauer noted: "Whether courts will see it the same way, given the various privacy protections Apple has implemented, is an interesting question, and one that is about to arise."

9to5Mac perspective

This is another example of the law failing to keep up with technology. If a recording is used to generate a text transcript or summary, but no one can directly access it, does that count as violating laws prohibiting recording? The short answer seems to be: no one knows.

Live Rewind in particular looks harmless. It can only record the last 15 seconds of conversation, and it emits a prompt sound each time it is activated, even if the watch is in silent mode or connected to headphones.

Ultimately this issue will likely need to be tested in court. The dilemma facing Apple Watch wearers is that if the court rules that the new features are subject to relevant laws, it is they themselves, not Apple, who will bear the legal responsibility.
